title: AI and You
text:
Welcome to AI and You
A mini-block class with Mr. Ross at Frederick Douglass High School

title: AI and You
text:
🧭 About the Class
AI is everywhere now. It writes, draws, talks, answers questions, and even pretends to be a friend. Some people say it thinks like a human brain. Is that true? In this class we will find out.
We will see what AI can do, learn the story of how it was built, look at how it works (and how it is a little like the brain in your head), and try it out for real tasks. By the end, you will know how to use AI well, spot it when it is wrong, and decide for yourself what you think about it and the world it is building.

title: AI and You
text:
👋 About Your Teacher
Before teaching, Mr. Ross spent over 15 years working in AI and data science, including time at Wolfram Research (the makers of Mathematica) and nearly a decade helping build a data science team at a Missouri company. He has a background in biology and statistics and still does AI work outside of school. He has been working with these tools since long before ChatGPT existed.

title: AI and You
text:
🎯 What You Will Learn

How to use AI tools for writing, school, art, and real-life problems.
The basic story of how AI was built and how it works.
How AI is and is not like the human brain.
How to catch AI when it makes things up or gets things wrong.
How AI is changing creativity, friendship, jobs, and the news.
What AI might mean for your future, and what you think about that.

title: 1.1 - What Is AI?
text:
🔥 Warm Up
Your phone opens when it sees your face. A video app knows what you want to watch next. A chatbot writes a story in two seconds.
All of these use AI. But what is AI? How is it different from a normal computer program? And is it like a human brain?
Today you sort things into AI and not AI. You try to teach a computer what a cat is. Then you play a drawing game against an AI.
Look at these 10 things. Which ones use AI?
Press a choice on each card: AI, Not AI, or Not sure. Talk with a partner. You do not need to agree.

title: 1.1 - What Is AI?
text:
👀 Show Mr. Ross's answers
    ↺ Start over
  






They all learn from examples, and they all make guesses.
The calculator and the alarm clock do not learn. They only follow rules that a person wrote.

title: 1.1 - What Is AI?
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.1.1 - What Does “AI” Mean?
AI means artificial intelligence.








Word
Meaning
Example




Artificial
made by people
Artificial flowers are made of plastic or paper.


Intelligence
the ability to learn, understand, and solve problems
You use intelligence to learn a new language.



So AI is a computer program that does things that usually need human thinking. AI can see faces, understand speech, translate languages, and write.
Most AI today does these things in a new way. It learns from examples. Let’s see why.



1.1.2 - Can You Write a Rule for “Cat”?
A normal computer program follows rules. A person writes every rule.



Program
A rule a person wrote




🔢 Calculator
If someone presses 2 + 3 =, show 5.


⏰ Alarm clock
If the time is 7:00, ring.



These rules are easy to write. Now try a hard one.

A computer gets a picture. Write a rule that tells the computer: Is this a cat?
Start like this: “It is a cat if it has …”
Write your rule on your sheet. Then test your rule on these three pictures. Does your rule give the right answer for each one?







Probably not. Many students write: “It is a cat if it has pointy ears, whiskers, and four legs.”

Picture B is a fox. It has pointy ears, whiskers, and four legs. The rule says “cat.” That is wrong.
Picture C is a cat. It is sleeping, so you cannot see its legs. The rule says “not a cat.” That is wrong too.

You can fix the rule. But then a new picture breaks it again.

For many years, scientists tried to build AI with rules. Rules worked for some jobs, like playing chess. Rules did not work well for seeing, hearing, or language. (You will learn this story in the next lessons.)
So scientists tried a different idea:

Do not write the rules.
Show the computer many examples. Each example has the right answer.
Let the computer find the pattern by itself.

This idea is called machine learning. The examples are called data.







Normal program: a person writes the rules. The computer follows them.
Machine learning: a person gives examples. The computer makes its own rules.





1.1.3 - AI Makes Predictions
Finish this sentence:

After school, I like to eat …

You did not know the answer from the sentence. You made a prediction. You used patterns from your own life.
AI makes predictions too.






A phone keyboard predicts your next word.
A video app predicts the next video you will like.
A chatbot predicts the next word of its answer. Then it predicts the next one. It does this again and again, very fast.


AI does not know the answer. It makes its best guess from patterns. Most of the time, the guess is good. Sometimes it is very wrong. In Unit 4, you will learn how to catch it.

title: 1.1 - What Is AI?
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.1.4 - Quick, Draw!
Quick, Draw! is a game made by Google. You draw. An AI tries to guess what you are drawing.
The AI learned from about 50 million drawings. People from all over the world made them.
✏️ Open Quick, Draw!


Click Let’s Draw!
The game shows a word. Draw it. You have 20 seconds. (If you do not know the word, ask a partner.)
Play all 6 rounds.
Write your results on your sheet. Did the AI guess? About how many seconds did it take?
At the end, click a drawing that the AI did not guess. Look at what the AI guessed.
Look at how other people drew the same thing.



The game saves your drawings and your country. Google shares the drawings with scientists around the world. Do not write your name or anything private in a drawing.


The AI learned from millions of drawings. Your first lines looked like the start of drawings it saw before. So it made a prediction. It did not wait for the whole picture.


Maybe your drawing was different from most people’s drawings. AI learns what is common in its data. When something is rare or different, AI often guesses wrong.
You will see this problem again in Unit 4, when we study bias.

On your sheet, circle one: Yes, A little, or No.

Tell a partner your answer and your reason.

I think AI is / is not / is a little like a human brain because …

I disagree with ___ because …

title: 1.2 - Can a Machine Think?
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 1950, a scientist named Alan Turing asked a big question: Can a machine think?
People do not agree on what “think” means. So Turing asked a new question that you can test: Can a machine talk so well that you cannot tell it is a machine?
He made a game to find out. Today, you play his game with a real AI.
Is it thinking? Mark each one on your sheet: Yes, No, or Not sure.
Compare with a partner.

title: 1.2 - Can a Machine Think?
text:
🔢
A calculator adds 375 + 498.


🐕
A dog finds its way home.


🔓
A phone opens when it sees your face.


🧩
You solve a puzzle.


🌻
A plant turns toward the sun.


💬
A chatbot writes a poem.





Probably not. People do not agree on what “thinking” means. Scientists still argue about it today.
Alan Turing saw this problem in 1950. So he did not try to define “thinking.” He made a test instead.

title: 1.2 - Can a Machine Think?
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.2.1 - Who Was Alan Turing?

Alan Turing was born in London in 1912. He was a mathematician.
In 1936, he wrote about a machine that could do any calculation if you gave it the right steps. Every computer today uses this idea.
In World War II, he helped break the secret code of the German military.
Today, his face is on the British 50 pound bank note.




1.2.2 - The Imitation Game
Turing called his test the imitation game. (To imitate means to copy someone.) Today, people call it the Turing test.






A judge sends questions to two hidden players, A and B.
One player is a person. One player is a machine.
The judge cannot see or hear them. The judge only reads their typed answers.
The judge decides: Which one is the machine?

If the judge cannot tell, the machine passes the test.

Turing said: in about 50 years, a judge will pick the right player 70 times out of 100, or less. The judge gets 5 minutes of questions.
So a machine passes if it fools the judge at least 30 times out of 100.




1.2.3 - Has a Machine Passed?
In 2025, scientists at the University of California, San Diego played Turing’s game. Almost 300 people were judges.
Each judge chatted with a person and a chatbot at the same time, for 5 minutes. Then the judge picked: Which one is the human?





GPT-4.5 was picked as the human 73% of the time. That is more often than the real humans were picked!
But there is a catch. The chatbot only did this well with a persona. The scientists told it: Act like a shy young person who uses slang.

A normal chatbot writes long, perfect answers. Real teenagers write short answers. They make spelling mistakes. They use slang.
The long, perfect answers were a clue. The persona hid the clue.

title: 1.2 - Can a Machine Think?
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.2.4 - Play the Imitation Game
Work in a group of 3 or 4. Each person has a job.

Group of 3: the judge also keeps score.
Only 4 or 5 in class? Play as one group. Everyone takes a turn as the judge.

🙋

Play 5 rounds. Then switch jobs.

    🙈 Judge, turn around. Then press here.

The AI answers in one second. A person needs time to type. AI helper: wait until the human player finishes. Then paste the AI’s answer.

Questions to try:

What did you eat for breakfast?
What is the weather outside right now?
What is 4,567 × 89? (A person needs a long time. Does the AI answer fast?)
Tell me about the room you are in.
Say “good morning” in your home language.


Questions about right here, right now often catch the AI. It cannot see the room or the weather. It has to make up an answer.
Hard math answered very fast is a clue too. So is perfect spelling.

title: 1.2 - Can a Machine Think?
text:
💬 Talk About It
Turing said: If you cannot tell the machine from a person, stop arguing about “thinking.”
Do you agree? If a machine fools you, does that mean it thinks?


If a machine fools me, it does / does not mean the machine thinks, because …
The best question to catch the AI was … because …
A person can … , but a chatbot cannot.
I think an AI should / should not have to tell you it is an AI, because …

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 1966, people at a university in Massachusetts talked to a computer program named ELIZA. ELIZA acted like a counselor. Some people told it their secrets. Some people believed it understood them.
ELIZA understood nothing. It followed a list of rules that one person wrote.
Today, you chat with ELIZA, read its rules, and write your own. Then you act out a famous puzzle: a person who answers notes in a language they do not know.
Work with a partner (or a group of 3, taking turns). One of you is ELIZA. ELIZA can only answer with the rule card. ELIZA cannot think of anything new!

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
If your partner says …
ELIZA says …




I feel ___
Why do you feel ___?


I am ___
How long have you been ___?


I want ___
Why do you want ___?


a word about family
Tell me more about your family.


anything else
Please go on.




Your partner tells ELIZA about their day. Talk for 3 turns.
Switch jobs.


Being ELIZA is easy. You do not need to understand anything. You only look for the key words and follow the card.
Sometimes ELIZA’s answer sounds caring. Sometimes it sounds strange. ELIZA cannot tell the difference.

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.3.1 - The Man Who Made ELIZA

Joseph Weizenbaum was born in Berlin, Germany, in 1923. His family was Jewish.
In 1936, his family escaped from the Nazis. They came to the United States.
He became a professor at MIT, a university near Boston.
In 1966, he shared ELIZA with the world. It was one of the first chatbots ever made.




1.3.2 - How ELIZA Works
ELIZA does not learn. Weizenbaum wrote every rule by hand. Here is how ELIZA answers one sentence:







ELIZA looks for key words. It does not know what the words mean.
If no rule matches, ELIZA says something that fits anything, like “Please go on.”
ELIZA is a normal program: a person wrote the rules (like the calculator in Lesson 1.1).





1.3.3 - People Believed It
Weizenbaum’s secretary knew that ELIZA was only a program. She watched him build it. But one day, she was chatting with ELIZA. She asked Weizenbaum to leave the room so she could talk to it alone.
Many people felt that ELIZA understood them. Today, we call this the ELIZA effect.
Weizenbaum was shocked. He became worried about computers. Later he wrote that some jobs should not be given to computers, even if a computer can do them.

Judges picked ELIZA as the human 23% of the time. A program from 1966 with no learning still fooled some people!

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.3.4 - Chat with ELIZA, Then Change Its Rules


Chat with ELIZA for 2 minutes.
Check the box Show which rule ELIZA used. Chat some more. Which rules does ELIZA use most?
Break ELIZA. Write something that makes ELIZA give a strange answer.
Open ELIZA’s rules. Add a new rule. Test it! (Example: when someone says i like *, ELIZA says Why do you like *?)
Add a rule in your home language. Does ELIZA answer you now?




  
  
    
    Send
  
   Show which rule ELIZA used

  
    📜 ELIZA's rules (open to read them and add your own)
    ELIZA checks the rules from the top. It uses the first rule that matches.
      A * means "the rest of the sentence." Put | between replies to give ELIZA a choice.
      Put / between words that mean the same thing, like mom/mother.
    
      When someone says: 
      ELIZA says: 
      ➕ Add my rule to the top
    
    
    ↺ Put back ELIZA's first rules
  






Do not tell ELIZA anything private. It is a game. (Nothing you type here leaves your computer.)
If you need to talk about something real, talk to a person: a teacher, the school counselor, or your family.


Nobody wrote rules in your language. ELIZA can only do what its rules say. A rule-based program knows nothing that a person did not write down.



1.3.5 - The Chinese Room

A philosopher named John Searle asked people to imagine this:

A person sits in a closed room. They do not know the language of the notes.
Notes come in through a slot.
The person has a rule book. It says: “If you see these shapes, send back those shapes.”
The person finds the shapes and copies the reply. They pass it out.
Outside, people who know the language read the replies. The replies make sense! They think someone in the room knows the language.

Does anyone in the room understand the language?

Act it out: the Klingon Room. Searle imagined notes in Chinese, a language he could not read. We will use Klingon. It is a language made up for the Star Trek TV shows and movies. (Some fans really speak it!)





Work in a group of 2 to 4: one person in the room, the rest outside. Each group needs one rule book and one set of note cards. (Only 4 in class? Be one group, and take turns going in the room.)


One person is in the room. Sit behind a folder or a book so the others cannot see you. Take the rule book.
Everyone else is outside. Share the note cards. Fold back the English part.
Pass one note into the room. The person in the room finds the note that looks exactly the same in the rule book. They copy the reply on the back. Pass it out.
Outside: check the reply with the English on your card. Does it make sense?
Do all 6 notes. Then switch: a new person goes in the room.



The room answered: “Yes. I am learning Klingon.”
But the person in the room does not know any Klingon. The answer sounds right, and it is not true.
Now look at the note about the bathroom. The room said: “I don’t understand.” That one is true! But the room only said it because a rule told it to.

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
💬 Talk About It
Searle said: the person in the room does not understand the language. They only follow rules. A computer is the same. It follows rules, so it does not understand anything.
Other people disagree. They say: maybe the person does not understand, but the whole room (the person plus the book) does.
What do you think?


The person in the room does / does not understand Klingon, because …
The whole room does / does not understand Klingon, because …
ELIZA is like the Klingon Room because …
Today’s chatbots are like / not like the Klingon Room, because …

title: 1.3 - The First Chatbot
text:
🚀 Go Further

With your group, write 10 new rules for a different job: a school helper, a soccer fan, or a food expert. Add them to ELIZA.
Then let another group chat with your ELIZA. How many turns until it says something strange?


Type the same sentence to ELIZA and to your class AI tool. Try: I feel nervous about my test.
Compare the two answers. Which one sounds like it understands? Does either one really understand? Write your reasons on your sheet.

More to explore

ELIZA Terminal: Chat with a version of ELIZA that works like the 1966 program. It looks like an old computer screen.

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
🔥 Warm Up
In 1958, a newspaper wrote about a new computer. It said the computer would soon “walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence.”
Did that happen? Not in 1958. Not for a long time.
For about 40 years, scientists tried to build AI out of rules. Rules did not work for seeing or talking. But rules did work for one thing: games. Today, you play a game against a bot made only of rules. Then you break it.
Long ago, people made big promises about AI. Read each one. Did it come true by the time they said? Mark your sheet.

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
Year
Who said it
The promise




A
1958
A newspaper
A new computer will soon walk, talk, see, write, make copies of itself, and know that it exists.


B
1958
Two scientists
Within 10 years, a computer will be the world chess champion.


C
1965
Herbert Simon
Within 20 years, machines will be able to do any work a person can do.


D
1970
Marvin Minsky
In 3 to 8 years, we will have a machine as smart as an average person.




None of them came true by the time they said.
Promise B came true later. A computer beat the world chess champion in 1997. That is 39 years later, not 10.
Promises C and D did not come true by the 1980s. Today, some people say AI is getting close to them. Other people strongly disagree. You will think about this in Unit 6.

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.4.1 - A New Name, Big Dreams
In 1955, four scientists wrote a plan for a summer meeting at Dartmouth College. In the plan, they used a new name: artificial intelligence. The meeting was in 1956. AI had a name.
The scientists had big dreams. They thought smart machines were only a few years away. Governments and companies gave them a lot of money.



1.4.2 - AI Winters
Progress was much slower than the promises. So the money stopped. This happened two times.
People call these times AI winters. (In winter, plants stop growing. In an AI winter, AI research stopped growing.)





In the 1980s, companies paid for AI built from rules. Experts wrote thousands of rules for jobs like checking orders or finding problems in machines. These programs were expensive. They broke when something new happened. Then came the second winter.

The promises in the Warm Up were hype: big promises, more than the facts showed. Hype brings money and attention. When the promises fail, people stop trusting the field.
People make big promises about AI today too. When you hear one, ask: Who says this? What do they get if I believe it?




1.4.3 - Rules Can Win at Games
A game is a small world. It has clear rules. Every move is on the board. Rules can work well in a small world.

In May 1997, IBM’s computer Deep Blue played the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. Deep Blue won, \(3\frac{1}{2}\) to \(2\frac{1}{2}\).

People wrote Deep Blue’s rules for judging a chess position.
Then it checked about 200 million positions every second.
Deep Blue did not learn like the drawing AI in Lesson 1.1. It used rules and speed.



Deep Blue could beat the best chess player in the world. But its rules could not tell a cat from a dog. Rules that work in a small world do not work in the big, messy real world.

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.4.4 - Beat the Rule Bot
This bot plays tic-tac-toe. It has 8 rules. It checks them in order and uses the first one it can.


Play 3 games with all the rules on. Can you beat the bot?
Turn off one rule. Play again. Can you beat it now?
Try different rules. Find the rules the bot needs most. Write them on your sheet.
Look at the orange box after each move. Which rule did the bot use?




  
    
    
      You are X. You go first.
      
      
        🙂 You won: 0
        🤖 Bot won: 0
        🤝 Tie: 0
      
      
        ↺ New game
         Bot goes first
      
    
  
  
    🤖 The bot's rules. It uses the first rule that it can use. Uncheck a rule to turn it off.
    
    If no rule works: pick any empty square.
  






No. With all 8 rules, the bot never loses. The best you can do is a tie. A computer played every possible game against it to check.
Some rules matter more than others. Turn off Block and the bot does not stop you from winning. But turn off Side and nothing changes, because the bot almost never needs it.


No one knows. People tried for years and could not write them. A cat can be any color, any size, in any position, in any light. There are too many cases.
That is why AI changed. In the next lesson, you will see what happened when scientists stopped writing rules and started collecting examples.

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
💬 Talk About It
Deep Blue beat the best chess player in the world. Is Deep Blue smart?


I think Deep Blue is / is not smart, because …
The most important rule for the bot was … because …
Rules work for games, but not for … , because …
People make big promises about AI because …

title: 1.4 - Rules Win at Games
text:
🚀 Go Further

Play tic-tac-toe on paper with a partner. One of you is the bot. The bot must follow the 8 rules on your sheet, in order. The bot cannot think! Can the human win? Switch jobs.


Write one promise about AI for 10 years from now. Use the form: “By 2036, AI will …” Mr. Ross keeps the promises. Will you be right, or will it be hype?


Write rules for a rock, paper, scissors bot. Then play against a partner who knows your rules. Can a bot that follows rules ever win at this game? Why or why not?

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
🔥 Warm Up
How did you learn what a dog is? Nobody gave you a rule. You saw many dogs: big dogs, small dogs, dogs in pictures, dogs on the street.
In 2006, a young scientist named Fei-Fei Li had an idea. Maybe computers need the same thing: not rules, but millions of examples.
Today, you do the job that thousands of people did for her project: you label pictures. And you find out that people do not always agree.
Think about something you learned to recognize as a child: a dog, a car, your mother’s voice, the letter A.
Tell a partner.

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
Did someone give you a rule? Or did you see many examples?
About how many examples do you think you saw?



A lot! Fei-Fei Li says: think of a child’s eyes as a camera that takes about 5 pictures every second. By age 3, the child has seen hundreds of millions of pictures. Children learn from examples, not rules.
Fei-Fei Li thought: computers have rules, but they do not have enough examples.

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.5.1 - Fei-Fei Li

Fei-Fei Li was born in Beijing, China, in 1976.
At 16, she moved to New Jersey with her mother to join her father.
Her family ran a dry-cleaning shop. She worked there on weekends in high school and in college.
She studied physics at Princeton University. Then she became an AI scientist.




1.5.2 - ImageNet
In 2006, Fei-Fei Li started a project called ImageNet. She wanted a giant dataset: pictures of everything in the world, each with a label.





The pictures came from the internet. But the internet does not say what is in each picture. People had to look and decide.
From 2008 to 2010, 49,000 people did this work online. Each person saw a word, like chair, and a group of pictures. They clicked every picture that showed a chair.
ImageNet was first shown to the world in 2009. It was the biggest set of labeled pictures anyone had made.



1.5.3 - The Big Win in 2012
Every year, scientists entered a contest. Their programs looked at ImageNet pictures and named what was in them.





In 2012, a team from Toronto used a neural network. (You will learn how neural networks work in Unit 2.) Their mistakes dropped from about 26% to 15%. Nobody had seen a jump that big.
They trained their network on two GPUs, chips made for video games. A GPU can do thousands of small math problems at the same time.
By 2015, the best AI made fewer mistakes than a person on this test!


Lots of data (like ImageNet)
Neural networks that learn from the data
Fast chips (GPUs) to do the math

AI did not get better because people wrote better rules. It got better because of examples.


Go is a board game from China. It is much harder for computers than chess. In 2016, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, one of the best Go players in the world, 4 games to 1.
AlphaGo first learned from 160,000 games played by people. Then it played millions of games against itself. In game 2, it made a move that surprised the experts. People still talk about move 37.

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.5.4 - Be the Labelers
Do the job of the ImageNet workers.


Pick a round: chair, sandwich, or car.
Work alone first. Click every picture that shows the word. Do not talk!
Press I’m done. Write your picture numbers on your sheet.
Compare with a partner (or a group of 3). Which pictures did you disagree on?
Do all 3 rounds.




  
  
  
  
    ✅ I'm done. Show my labels.
    ↺ Clear
  
  





Class vote. Mr. Ross picks the hardest picture. Everyone votes. How many said yes? How many said no?

There is no right answer! People decide. And different people decide differently.
ImageNet had this problem too. So the workers got instructions, and several people labeled each picture. If most people agreed, the label stayed.


If the labelers said a hot dog is a sandwich, the AI will say it too. The AI does not know what a sandwich really is. It only knows what people labeled.
What if all the labelers came from one country? You will think about this in Unit 4.

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
💬 Talk About It
49,000 people labeled ImageNet. Most people do not know their names. The scientists became famous.


The people who labeled the data should / should not get credit, because …
People disagreed about picture … because …
If the labelers all came from one country, the AI might …
The most important part of the new recipe is … because …

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
📺 Watch


The talk is 18 minutes. In class, we watch the first part.
While you watch: Fei-Fei Li compares computers to children. What do children do that computers could not?
Captions in your language: Press CC to turn on captions. Then press ⚙️ Settings, then Subtitles/CC, then Auto-translate. Choose your language.

title: 1.5 - Data Changes Everything
text:
🚀 Go Further

Why do GPUs help? Try it with your class.

Mr. Ross writes 24 easy addition problems.
One student solves all 24 alone. Time it.
Everyone else shares the next 24 problems. Each person does a few, all at the same time. Time it.
Which was faster? A normal computer chip is like the one fast student. A GPU is like the whole class.

(Only 4 in class? One student against a team of 3 still works.)


Write a rule for sandwich that ends the argument. Test it on all 12 pictures. Does your rule work for every picture? Does everyone in your group agree with it?


Google DeepMind made a film about the AlphaGo match. Watch the part about move 37 and how Lee Sedol felt.
AlphaGo, the full film (YouTube)

More to explore

Quick, Draw! The Data: Pick a word. Look at how thousands of people drew it. Would you label every drawing the same way?

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
🔥 Warm Up
On November 30, 2022, a company called OpenAI shared a chatbot named ChatGPT. In about two months, around 100 million people used it. At that time, no app had ever grown that fast.
ChatGPT came from an idea that Google scientists shared in 2017. The idea is called attention. You use it every time you read.
Today, you see how attention works. You build a sentence the way a chatbot does: one word at a time. Then you finish the class timeline, from 1950 to today.
Read these two sentences. What does “it” mean in each one? Write your answers on your sheet.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.
The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too wide.



In sentence 1, “it” means the animal. Animals get tired. Streets do not.
In sentence 2, “it” means the street. Streets can be wide. Animals are not “too wide” to cross.
Only one word changed. To decide, you looked back at other words in the sentence. You paid attention to the right words.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
👥 Learn Together

1.6.1 - Attention (2017)
For a long time, AI read one word at a time. It had trouble remembering the start of a long sentence. In 2017, scientists at Google shared a new kind of neural network. They called it the transformer.
A transformer looks at every word at the same time. For each word, it decides which other words matter most. This is called attention. The scientists’ paper had a famous title: Attention Is All You Need.








1.6.2 - GPT and ChatGPT





A GPT is a large language model. It learned by playing one game, billions of times: predict the next word (like the phone keyboard in Lesson 1.1). When it answers you, it predicts one word, then the next, then the next.

There are many chatbots built this way: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Llama, and more. Most AI tools made for schools are built on top of models like these.




1.6.3 - AI Wins Nobel Prizes (2024)
The Nobel Prize is one of the biggest prizes in science. In 2024, two Nobel Prizes went to AI.

Physics: John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton, for early discoveries that made neural networks possible.
Chemistry: Demis Hassabis and John Jumper, for AlphaFold. It is an AI that predicts the shape of proteins (the tiny machines inside your body). They shared the prize with David Baker, who designs new proteins.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
🛠️ Try It

1.6.4 - See the Attention
Click the word that “it” means. Then change the last word. Watch which words light up.


  
  What does "it" mean? Click the word you think. Then change the last word and try again.
  
  
  
  This shows the idea. A real transformer gives a number to every pair of words, and it does this many times at once.








1.6.5 - Be the Chatbot: Next Word, by Vote
A chatbot writes one word at a time. It picks a word that is likely to come next. Now the class does the same thing.


Mr. Ross writes the start of a sentence on the board: After school, my friends and I …
Everyone writes one next word on a small paper. Do not talk!
Mr. Ross counts the words. The word with the most votes goes on the board.
Do it again for the next word. Keep going until the sentence ends (about 8 words).
Now give the same start to your class AI tool: “Finish this sentence: After school, my friends and I”. Compare its sentence with the class sentence.



With only 4 or 5 people, many words get 1 vote. Break a tie by rolling a die, or ask everyone to write two words each.


Usually it is ordinary. The most common word wins every time, so the sentence uses common words.
Chatbots have the same problem. So they do not always pick the top word. Sometimes they pick the second or third word, on purpose, to make the writing more interesting.



1.6.6 - Finish the Class Timeline
Put every card from Unit 1 on the wall, in order. Is anything missing? With a partner, pick one card and explain it to the class in 2 sentences.



Year
What happened




1950
Alan Turing asks: Can a machine think?


1956
AI gets its name at Dartmouth College.


1966
ELIZA, one of the first chatbots.


1980
The Chinese Room.


1997
Deep Blue beats the world chess champion.


2009
ImageNet: 14 million labeled pictures.


2012
A neural network wins the ImageNet contest.


2016
AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol at Go.


2017
Transformers and attention.


2022
ChatGPT.


2024
Nobel Prizes for AI.


2025
A chatbot passes the Turing test.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
💬 Talk About It
ChatGPT learned from text that people wrote: books, websites, news, and more. Most of those writers were never asked.


Writers should / should not be asked before AI learns from their words, because …
The most important moment on our timeline is … because …
In 10 years, I think AI will … , because …

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
📺 Watch


While you watch: How does a chatbot decide which word comes next?
Captions in your language: Press CC to turn on captions. Then press ⚙️ Settings, then Subtitles/CC, then Auto-translate. Choose your language.

title: 1.6 - Transformers and ChatGPT
text:
🚀 Go Further

Write your own tricky “it” sentence, where one word changes what “it” means. Ask your class AI tool: “In this sentence, what does ‘it’ mean?” Does it get it right? Try your sentence in your home language too.


With a partner, make a poster about one person from Unit 1: Alan Turing, Joseph Weizenbaum, John Searle, Fei-Fei Li, Geoffrey Hinton, or Demis Hassabis. Where were they from? What did they do? Hang it next to their card on the timeline.

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Unit 2: Brains and Neural Networks
A real look at how brain cells work, and how computer scientists copied the idea to build AI.
We will act out a neural network as a class, watch one learn on screen, and train our own. Then we will see how the same idea works inside AI that sees pictures and AI that writes.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Explain how a brain cell (neuron) sends a signal
Explain how practice changes the brain
Explain how an artificial neuron copies that idea
Train a neural network and watch it learn
Explain how AI sees pictures and how a chatbot picks its next word

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Unit 3: Using AI Well
The heart of the class. You will learn how to ask AI good questions. You will use it to help with writing, research, translation, math, and art.
Then you will finish a real project that uses AI to do something useful in your life. We will have time to get feedback, make it better, and do the work right.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Write clear prompts and make them better
Use AI to help with writing, research, translation, math, and art
Check AI’s work before you use it
Use AI honestly in school
Finish a real project that uses AI to solve a problem in your life

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn

AI lies, AI is biased, and AI can be used to fake pictures, videos, and voices. We will learn how to catch it, how to check its work, and why “AI cheat detectors” do not really work.
You will build your own toolkit for spotting AI-generated content.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

title: Introduction

Catch AI when it makes things up

Spot fake pictures, videos, and voices

What You’ll Learn

What AI means for your privacy, your future job, and the news you see.
We will look at real scams, real changes happening at work right now, and have honest conversations about what is coming.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to:

Protect your privacy when you use apps and AI

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Unit 6: AI and Our Future
AI can write poems, make art, and act like a friend. It also uses energy and water, and it depends on people’s work. Who decides how it is used? Where is all of this going?
We will talk about AI art, AI friends, the hidden costs of AI, the rules for AI, and possible futures. At the end, we come back to the question from the first day.

title: Glossary
text:
AI winter
A time when people stopped giving money to AI research, because AI did not do what people promised. There were AI winters in the 1970s and around 1990.
See Also: hype



artificial intelligence (AI)
A computer program that does things that usually need human thinking, like seeing, talking, translating, or making choices. Most AI today learns from examples.

Example:
Face unlock on a phone, a translation app, and a chatbot all use AI.

See Also: machine learning, computer program



attention
In a transformer, the way the AI looks at all the other words to decide which ones matter most for each word.

Example:
In “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired,” attention connects “it” to “animal.”

See Also: transformer



chatbot
An AI program that you talk to with words. You type or say something, and it answers.

Example:
ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are chatbots.

See Also: artificial intelligence, prediction



computer program
A list of steps that a computer follows. Apps and games are computer programs.
See Also: rule



data
Information, like pictures, words, numbers, or sounds. An AI learns from data.

Example:
The Quick, Draw! AI learned from data: about 50 million drawings.

See Also: machine learning



dataset
A big collection of examples that an AI learns from, like pictures with labels.

Example:
ImageNet is a dataset of 14 million labeled pictures.

See Also: data, label



Deep Blue
A chess computer made by IBM. In 1997, it beat the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov. It used rules that people wrote, and it checked about 200 million chess positions every second.
See Also: rule



ELIZA effect
When people feel that a computer understands them, but it does not. It is named after ELIZA, a chatbot from 1966.

Example:
ELIZA only followed rules, but some people told it their secrets.

See Also: chatbot



GPU
A computer chip first made for video games. It can do thousands of small math problems at the same time, so it is very good for training neural networks. GPU means “graphics processing unit.”
See Also: neural network



hype
Big promises and excitement, more than the facts show.

Example:
In 1970, a scientist said that a machine as smart as a person was 3 to 8 years away. That was hype.

See Also: AI winter



judge
In the Turing test, the person who asks the questions and decides which player is the machine.
See Also: Turing test



key word
A word that a program looks for to decide what to do.

Example:
When you type “I feel,” ELIZA finds the key words “I feel” and uses its rule for them.

See Also: rule



label
The right answer that a person attaches to an example, like “cat” on a picture of a cat. An AI learns from examples and their labels.

Example:
In ImageNet, people from 167 countries labeled 14 million pictures.

See Also: dataset



large language model
A transformer trained on a huge amount of text to predict the next word. Chatbots like ChatGPT are built on large language models. People often call them LLMs.
See Also: transformer, prediction, chatbot



machine learning
A way to make AI. People do not write the rules. They give the computer many examples, and the computer finds the patterns by itself.
See Also: data, pattern, rule



neural network
A kind of AI made of many small parts that work a little like brain cells. Each part does a tiny bit of math. A neural network learns from examples.
See Also: machine learning, GPU



pattern
Something that is the same, or repeats, in many examples.

Example:
In most drawings of a cat, the ears are two triangles on top of the head. That is a pattern.




persona
A character that someone pretends to be. You can tell an AI to use a persona, like “Act like a 15-year-old student.”

Example:
In a 2025 Turing test, a chatbot with a persona fooled judges much more often than the same chatbot without one.

See Also: Turing test



prediction
A best guess about something you do not know yet. A prediction can be wrong.

Example:
A phone keyboard makes a prediction about your next word.




rule
An exact instruction that a computer follows: “If this happens, do that.” In a normal computer program, a person writes the rules.

Example:
An alarm clock follows one rule: “If the time is 7:00, ring.”

See Also: computer program, machine learning



transformer
A kind of neural network, first shared by Google scientists in 2017. It uses attention to connect the words in a sentence. It is the T in GPT.
See Also: attention, neural network, large language model



Turing test
A game Alan Turing described in 1950. He called it the imitation game. A judge chats in writing with a person and a machine. If the judge cannot tell which one is the machine, the machine passes.
See Also: judge, chatbot



understand
To know what something means, not only what it looks like. Whether AI can understand is a question people still argue about.

Example:
In the Klingon Room, the person copies correct replies in Klingon, but they do not understand Klingon.

See Also: ELIZA effect
